title: TDDR Rising Narratives — Sunday evening, Nov 22
summary: A snapshot of opposition narratives from the Right and the Far Left as of 5:20 PM ET Sunday, Nov 22, 2026. Built for TDDR (Too Dumb Didn't Read). Sunday's shows drove the day. On the Far Left, Medicare for All was again the biggest query (29,334 posts in 24 hours, 2.36× its prior daily average; 16,533 from 7 AM to 5 PM versus 5,799 the same hours Saturday) after Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed took his 'TrumpCare' pitch to Meet the Press and said he would accept a version that keeps private plans. Van Hollen vs. Schumer nearly tripled in daytime hours (6,979 versus 2,415) after Trump said Schumer would be 'very hard' to work with and Van Hollen claimed 'north of 15' votes. On the Right, Trump posted that stocks lost '$6 trillion' and the Nasdaq is 'down 20%' since the midterms, '100% due' to Democrats; the Nasdaq Composite is down about 10% since the last pre-election close. Two new Right cards: a 2020 Marco Rubio video, 'Democratic socialism… is Marxism,' went viral again (5,305 posts, 28.73×, from one 104,951-view post), and Obama's 'golf country club' line about House Republicans (1,241 posts, 11.06×). Impeachment talk rose after Jeffries said Hegseth 'should be impeached' if Trump won't remove him. The Rikers and 'nullify the midterms' stories cooled. Two faded cards were dropped. No political topic was on the U.S. X trends list this evening. Every count, quote and fact-check comes from sources and X queries pulled this evening or carried over from this morning and labeled. Nothing here is invented.

NFL Sunday dominated: 'Steelers' (40,802 posts), 'Bears' (39,756), 'Eagles' (34,641), 'Broncos' (33,651), 'Ravens' (30,966), 'Titans' (25,724) and 'Saints' (24,642), plus anime ('Naruto,' 87,676; 'Luffy,' 63,092), 'Tom Jackson' (58,602) and 'Swift' (56,855). 'McCarthy' (9,124) appeared among the NFL trends; we did not score it. No trend related to a U.S. opposition narrative, so no card received the trend bonus. Several trend objects had no tweet_count ('David Bailey,' 'Abdul Carter,' '#BigBlue,' 'Overshown,' 'Vita Vea,' 'Spencer Anderson'); their volumes are unavailable and we did not estimate them.

oppositionNote.body: Right = narratives the Right is pushing after the Democratic midterm wave. Far Left = pressure on Democratic leadership and the incoming majority from the party's left. The Rikers card is a Right attack on a Democratic mayor; we include it because Mamdani is being used as the national face of the party. The market card is tagged Right because the 'Democrats crashed the market' frame comes from Trump and the Right, even though many posts matching the query are rebuttals. The immigration card is tagged Right because the 'replacing Black voters' frame is the Right's reading of Stephen A. Smith's comments; Smith is a Democratic voter. The new Rubio card is tagged Right because it recasts the incoming majority as Marxist, using a 2020 video. The new Obama card is tagged Right because the backlash, not Obama's remark, is the narrative. The Medicare for All card is tagged Far Left because the pressure is on Jeffries, Schumer and the incoming majority to deliver it now, even though Trump amplified the pitch. The Van Hollen card is tagged Far Left because the push to replace Schumer comes from the party's left, even though Trump weighed in. The tag is the primary opposition frame.

methodology: Last updated Sunday, Nov 22, 2026, 5:20 PM ET. This is a research snapshot for TDDR, not a live API, and it will go stale. U.S. X trends were pulled at about 5:06 PM ET. This morning's snapshot (Nov 22, 7:25 AM ET) is kept in the archive and was not overwritten. Eight of its ten narratives were re-counted with the same queries so momentum compares like with like. The new 24-hour window overlaps this morning's by 14 hours (5 PM Saturday to 7 AM Sunday ET), so we also report each query's 7 AM–5 PM ET daytime count against the same hours on Saturday. Two narratives were dropped because they faded: the popular-vote compact card (2,231 posts in the last 24 hours, 0.52× its prior daily average; 939 from 7 AM to 5 PM ET versus 1,958 the same hours Saturday) and the 'Social Security is a Ponzi scheme' card (1,302 posts, 0.55×; 505 versus 1,357). Two were added with new queries: the resurfaced Rubio 'democratic socialism is Marxism' video and the backlash to Obama's 'golf country club' remark. Other candidates were counted and not carved out as cards: the Senate filibuster debate, including Van Hollen's talk of ending it (2,679 posts, 1.24×; 976 from 7 AM to 5 PM versus 2,018 Saturday); Jeffries and the Iran war funding fight (498 posts, 0.40×); 'Democrats will raise your taxes' after incoming Ways and Means Chairman Richard Neal promised hearings on Trump's tax cuts (412 posts, 0.47×); and streamer Hasan Piker's remarks about older Black voters (331 posts, 7.07× a small baseline). The Bartow, Florida, city-meeting protest of an imam's prayer and Stewart Rhodes's break with Trump were covered by X News but are not opposition narratives about Democrats, so we did not count them.

For each narrative we ran one English-language X search with x.get_posts_counts_recent at hourly granularity over a 166-hour window from 7:00 PM ET Sunday, Nov 15, through 5:00 PM ET Sunday, Nov 22 (the 'seven-day' total; the API's recent-search limit is seven days back from the pull). The last 24 hourly buckets (5:00 PM ET Saturday, Nov 21, through 5:00 PM ET Sunday, Nov 22) give the 24-hour count, and the hourly buckets were summed into UTC days for the daily charts. We counted named news or fact-check outlets whose coverage we opened or retrieved and cite on the card. Official government pages, bill text, transcripts, advocacy groups, research groups, blogs, X News summaries, archives and X posts are cited as sources but not counted as outlets; MODEL is cited on the market card but not counted, and the February 2020 articles on the Rubio card are cited only to date the video. This evening we researched the two new cards and re-researched the Medicare for All, Van Hollen, market and impeachment cards; the other cards carry this morning's outlet counts and say so. No topic in this set appeared on the U.S. trends list at about 5:06 PM ET.

Score = 50% volume index + 30% acceleration index + 20% coverage index. Volume index is 100 × log10(1 + last-24h posts) / log10(1 + the highest last-24h count in this set). Acceleration index is 100 × min(last-24h / prior daily average, 3) / 3, so a triple-or-higher average scores 100. Prior daily average is (seven-day total − last 24h) / 6. Coverage index is 70 × min(outlets, 7) / 7, plus 30 if the topic was on the U.S. X trends list this evening. No card got the trend bonus. The Rubio and Obama queries had tiny baselines, so their acceleration indexes are maxed out; the Rubio card has no counted outlets because we found no current coverage of the clip. The Rikers, Van Hollen and 'nullify' queries carry last week's spikes in their seven-day totals, which keeps their acceleration low. Read the post counts alongside the scores. Morning-to-evening score changes also reflect the higher volume ceiling (29,334 this evening versus 18,647 this morning) and how much coverage we retrieved.

Counts are query matches, not unique posts or unique users, and queries can overlap. The audit query overlaps the 'nullify' query and also catches posts mocking the demand. The market query requires a market term plus 'Democrats' or 'blue wave,' so it also catches rebuttals and general market posts that mention Democrats. The Rikers query also catches straight news posts and rebuttals. The Medicare for All query catches supporters, opponents and general health-care posts, and its 'M4A' term can catch unrelated uses. The Van Hollen query catches syndicated news posts. The immigration query includes the phrase 'Stephen A,' so it can catch unrelated Stephen A. Smith posts. The impeachment query also catches Democrats discussing impeachment, and this evening much of it was about Hegseth, not Trump. The Rubio query catches any post pairing 'democratic socialism' with Marxism or communism, including posts from other countries. The Obama query can catch older posts' quotes and unrelated golf talk. Replies are included, and automated @grok replies make up a visible share of several queries. Sentiment is a qualitative label from relevancy-sorted post samples and from quotes in news coverage, not a scientific poll. This evening we pulled fresh samples for the Medicare for All, Van Hollen, market, audit, immigration, impeachment, Rubio and Obama queries. The Rikers and 'nullify' cards carry this morning's sentiment and say so. Daily bar charts use UTC days (a UTC day starts at 7:00 PM ET the previous evening). Bars marked * are partial windows. Hourly charts are labeled in ET.

disinfo.caveatBody: New this evening: Trump's 'NASDAQ, by itself, is down 20%' since the Nov. 3 midterms is wrong. From the last close before the vote (Nov. 2) to Friday's close the Nasdaq Composite fell 10.1%, the S&P 500 8.4% and the Dow 7.4% (Mediaite; MODEL, checking Nasdaq index data); the Composite is 18.1% below its Oct. 6 record, and the Nasdaq-100 is 19.8% below its record. '100% due to the Democrats' leaves out the AI and chip sell-off and the turmoil at Nvidia that coverage ties last week's drop to (The Hill), and the new Congress is not sworn in until Jan. 3, 2027. The viral Marco Rubio 'Democratic socialism… is Marxism' video is from Feb. 24, 2020, when he was a senator commenting on Bernie Sanders's primary campaign (Political Wire; The Right Scoop), not a response to this month's election. 'Jeffries will impeach Hegseth' is closer to his words than the headlines: he told The New York Times Hegseth 'should be impeached if Donald Trump fails to remove him'; no articles have been filed. 'El-Sayed abandoned Medicare for All' is overstated: he said on Meet the Press he supports Sanders's bill but prefers a version that keeps private plans available (NBC News; POLITICO). Carried over from this morning: 'Forensic-audit all 50 states before certifying' is misleading. Every state already has a post-election audit procedure (NCSL, via Votebeat), Texas began its first statewide risk-limiting audit of the U.S. Senate race on Nov. 19 (Houston Public Media), and audits and certification are separate processes that can run in parallel (The Crosscheck, which rated the 'don't certify until verified' claim Misleading). Earlier viral fraud claims, a Houston 'FBI raid' and a Wyandot County, Ohio, tally error, were debunked by PolitiFact and AFP. 'Medicare for All saves 114,000 lives and $1 trillion a year' is a projection from a Yale preprint that has not been peer reviewed; about 51,300 of those lives come from reversing coverage cuts enacted since 2025, not from single-payer itself, and the model leaves out transition costs (Yale School of Public Health; Renaissance Physician). Trump's 'Democrats Hurt Stocks' chart gets the numbers right and the cause wrong. The S&P 500 did fall 8.7% from the Nov. 3 close to the Nov. 20 close, and total U.S.-listed market value fell about $7.7 trillion (Candid Dragon's chatter check), but stocks rallied the day after the results, Friday's drop is tied mainly to the Nvidia accounting-probe report and the AI sell-off (Reuters; CNBC), and the new Congress is not sworn in until Jan. 3, 2027. 'Democrats are importing immigrants to replace Black voters' is Stephen A. Smith's stated belief, not an established fact: the census does count every resident for House seats, as the Constitution requires, but noncitizens cannot vote in federal elections (18 U.S.C. § 611), and PolitiFact has rated the related claim that millions of immigrants are registering to vote Pants on Fire. 'Trump endorsed Medicare for All' is overstated: he reposted El-Sayed's 'TrumpCare' card and praised Democrats' health-care ideas but has not backed a bill. 'Mamdani is releasing thousands of criminals' and 'Mamdani is closing Rikers now' get the plan backward: it sets a target of no more than 4,100 people in custody by the end of 2032, reached through diversion and shorter case delays, keeps Rikers open until borough jails are built, and asks the City Council to move the legal deadline later, from August 2027 to 2032 (City of New York; City & State; Gothamist). The 'nullify the midterms' demand is still circulating as a phone script; the president has no authority to cancel state results or declare martial law (Brennan Center; Protect Democracy), and fact-checkers found no evidence that machines switched votes. 'The Protect Our Neighbors Act gives 1.6 million people green cards' is misleading; 'Democrats are already preparing a third impeachment' of Trump is a prediction by Jim Jordan, not a report.

Asked whether he backs Sen. Bernie Sanders's bill, which would replace most private insurance, he said he does but prefers a version 'like public schools,' with public coverage guaranteed and private plans still available (NBC News; POLITICO). The query hit 2,848 posts in the 2 PM hour, its busiest of the window. Critics on the left said that version is a public option, not single payer; critics on the right said he is already backing off. From 5 PM ET Saturday to 7 AM ET Sunday the query matched 12,836 posts, versus 6,750 in the same hours a night earlier. Rising overnight. New this morning: this is now the largest query in the set, and its overnight count nearly doubled the night before. X News stories kept the 'TrumpCare' card moving (Trump reposted Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed's mock gold cards on Truth Social without comment), and Sen. Elizabeth Warren urged Democrats to pass health care and child care expansions on their own votes and see if Trump vetoes them (X News). Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez's hope for a 'first phase' under the new majority drew fire from parts of the left as a retreat, while defenders noted Sen. Bernie Sanders's bill is itself phased (X News). A Yale School of Public Health preprint, which has not been peer reviewed, projects single-payer would cut national health spending by about $1.04 trillion a year and save about 114,000 lives (Yale School of Public Health; Scientific American); per X News, Sanders and Rep. Ro Khanna promoted it. A physician's critique notes about 51,300 of those lives come from reversing coverage cuts enacted since 2025, not from single-payer itself, and that the model leaves out transition costs (Renaissance Physician). We added Scientific American to the outlet count.
talkingPoints: Yale says Medicare for All saves $1 trillion and 114,000 lives a year. What are we waiting for?
Pass it with Democratic votes and dare Trump to veto it.
Even Trump says Democrats have good points on health care — pass Medicare for All.
Put his name on it if that's what it takes: TrumpCare for All.
Leadership and the 2028 hopefuls are out of excuses.
Deliver popular policies like Medicare for All, or the Republican majority comes back.
narratives.amplifiers: Left: Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (@AbdulElSayed), Sen. Bernie Sanders, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez ('first phase' push, per X News), streamer Hasan Piker (via @socialistadri, 24,287 views), Common Dreams and Daily Kos. Aggregators: @Popstonox (372,266 views). Trump himself amplified the pitch on Truth Social. Opposition from parts of Trump's base in replies.
narratives.whyItWorks: It is a rare moment when the left's signature demand seems to have the president's blessing, so it turns an old wish into a test of the new Democratic majority: if Trump is open, any delay looks like leadership's choice. The gold-card gag is funny, visual and easy to share, and the left gets to troll Trump and pressure Jeffries and Schumer in the same post. Broad public support for guaranteed coverage in polls gives it a majority-sounding frame.
narratives.audience: Progressive and DSA-aligned voters, Sanders and El-Sayed supporters, young voters who follow streamers like Hasan Piker, and health-cost-stressed independents; Trump's base is the hostile audience in replies.
narratives.counter: Take the opening seriously and make Trump own it: ask him to back specific steps Democrats can pass in the first 100 days, such as restoring the ACA tax credits and lowering drug prices, and then build toward broader coverage. Be honest that a repost is not a bill and that a full single-payer system needs 60 Senate votes or a rules change. The win for Democrats is a health-cost vote Trump can't veto without breaking his own word.

factChecks.detail: Trump reposted a screenshot of El-Sayed's post with the 'TrumpCare' card on Truth Social on Nov. 21 after saying Democrats 'have some good points on healthcare' and that a bipartisan deal could produce 'great healthcare' (The Washington Times; Mediaite). We found no statement from Trump backing a specific Medicare for All bill or single-payer design. This is TDDR's read of the reporting, not a rating from a fact-check outlet.

narratives.title: Stephen A. Smith: 'You secure that voting bloc, you don't need the Black vote' — the 'Democrats are importing voters' card grows to 5.36× its baseline

narratives.sentiment: Triumphant on the Right ('Stephen A. just said the quiet part out loud'); replacement framing aimed at Black voters, with some Black users pushing back
narratives.sentimentNote: In a relevancy sample of posts from 7 AM to 5 PM ET Sunday, the top post was @LFRFamily ('They understand now that the Democrats are replacing us with new voters and workers,' 426 likes, 10,641 views), followed by @Newsforce (2,738 views) and smaller 'said the quiet part' posts. A Gateway Pundit headline ('Democrats' Diabolical Plan to REPLACE Them With Illegal Aliens via Census Apportionment') circulated. This is a read of that sample, not a poll.
narratives.summary: Evening update (Nov 22): 5,432 posts in the last 24 hours, 2.72 times the prior daily average (this morning: 7,192 and 5.36×). From 7 AM to 5 PM ET Sunday the query matched 2,221 posts, versus 3,980 in the same hours Saturday. Cooling in daytime hours. Still well above its baseline but cooling in daytime hours. X News posted a new story ('Stephen A. Smith Questions Democrats' Immigration Strategy in Barbershop Talk') at about 2:25 PM ET. We pulled a fresh sample but did not add outlets this evening. This morning's card (7:25 AM ET): Morning update (Nov 22): 7,192 posts in the last 24 hours, 5.36 times the prior daily average (last evening: 5,095 and 4.38×). From 5 PM ET Saturday to 7 AM ET Sunday the query matched 3,212 posts, versus 1,115 in the same hours a night earlier. Rising overnight. New this morning: the clip kept spreading overnight, with nearly three times the posts of the night before. The most-viewed post in our overnight sample was '🚨Report: Stephen A. Smith is going viral for saying Democrats are using illegal immigrants to replace Black voters' (@TheCalvinCooli1, 6,174 views), followed by an attack on the Protect Our Neighbors Act's 'ticket to a green card' (@FloppingAces, 3,940 views). The bill, introduced by Rep. Lateefah Simon with fellow California Democrats, would make final removal orders expire after 10 years unless the Department of Homeland Security shows clear and convincing evidence to renew them; it is a proposal, not law (Local News Matters; Rep. Simon's office). We added Local News Matters to the outlet count.
talkingPoints: Even Stephen A. says it: Democrats use immigration to secure a voting bloc so they don't need the Black vote.
The census counts illegal immigrants, so open borders buy blue states more House seats and electoral votes.
Democrats take Black voters for granted and are replacing them.
Democrats just filed amnesty: ignore a deportation order for 10 years and you get a green card.
They ran on affordability, and the first bill is for illegal immigrants.
narratives.amplifiers: Right: @bennyjohnson (87,648 views), @EricLDaugh (76,687), @MarioNawfal (37,246), @DefiantLs, @GuntherEagleman, @RealAmVoice, PJ Media, and former Border Patrol official Gregory Bovino ('Stephen A. is right… It's YOUR vote'). Origin: Stephen A. Smith's Nov. 18 'Straight Shooter' episode filmed at a Washington, D.C., barbershop. Pushback: commentator Roland Martin (per ProfiloPolitics). Bill thread carried over from this morning: @ElectionWiz, @RedWavePress, @Bubblebathgirl.
narratives.whyItWorks: A lifelong Democratic voter and one of the most famous Black media figures in the country gives the Right a messenger it cannot be accused of inventing, and the clip was filmed in a Black barbershop. It mixes a real grievance (Democrats taking Black loyalty for granted) and a real fact (the census counts all residents for House seats) with an unproven motive, so each step sounds reasonable. It lands three days after the Protect Our Neighbors Act gave the 'amnesty' frame a news peg.
narratives.audience: Black men who follow Smith and feel taken for granted by Democrats, immigration-restriction voters, sports-media audiences who don't follow politics closely, and Right influencers' X followings.
narratives.counter: Don't argue with Smith's frustration; agree that Democrats have to earn Black votes on prices, jobs and safety, which is what he actually asked for. Then separate the facts: noncitizens cannot vote in federal elections (18 U.S.C. § 611), and while the census does count every resident for apportionment, that rule is in the Constitution, not a Democratic plan. Smith himself says he doesn't want law-abiding, tax-paying migrants deported. On the bill: an order has to be 10 years old, the person needs 10 years of continuous presence and no serious conviction, and a judge can renew the order (bill text; ABC News).

factChecks.claim: The Protect Our Neighbors Act gives green cards to 1.6 million people with deportation orders.
factChecks.detail: The bill's sponsor puts the number of people with final removal orders at about 1.19 million; 1.6 million is an earlier ICE figure. The bill would let an order expire only after 10 years, allow a judge to renew it, and let a person petition for any status they are eligible for only after 10 years of continuous presence and no conviction for a crime punishable by more than a year. It does not hand out green cards automatically, and it has no path in the current Republican House. This is TDDR's read of the bill text and Simon's release, not a rating from a fact-check outlet.

factChecks.claim: The Protect Our Neighbors Act would wipe out 1.6 million deportation orders.
factChecks.detail: About 1.6 million people have final removal orders (ICE testimony cited by ABC News), but the bill covers only orders at least 10 years old for people continuously present with no criminal conviction, and a judge could renew an order. No count of who would qualify has been published. This is TDDR's read of that reporting, not a rating from a fact-check outlet.

factChecks.claim: Democrats are bringing in immigrants so they can vote for Democrats.
factChecks.rating: Pants on Fire (PolitiFact, on a related claim)
factChecks.detail: PolitiFact rated Trump's claim that millions of immigrants are signing up to vote illegally Pants on Fire. Noncitizens, including green-card holders, cannot vote in federal elections under 18 U.S.C. § 611, and PolitiFact has found noncitizen voting rare. PolitiFact has not rated Smith's remarks or the new bill.

From 7 AM to 5 PM ET Sunday the query matched 6,979 posts, versus 2,415 in the same hours Saturday. Rising in daytime hours. New this evening: Trump wrote on Truth Social Sunday morning that 'it is going to be very hard for me to work with Chuck Schumer should he become Senate Majority Leader,' calling him 'one of the worst in history' (The Epoch Times; The Hill). On NBC's Meet the Press, Van Hollen said his support is 'north of 15 and momentum is in our direction,' said Trump's post was not an endorsement ('I have fought him tooth and nail'), and called the race about 'economic populism' (NBC News). He needs 28 votes in the Dec. 1 secret ballot; The Hill's whip list shows 15 public backers for Schumer and five for Van Hollen, and Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.) praised Van Hollen on CNN (The Hill). The query's busiest hour was 12 PM Sunday (875 posts). This morning's card (7:25 AM ET): Morning update (Nov 22): 9,380 posts in the last 24 hours, 0.79 times the prior daily average (last evening: 4,442 and 0.33×). Gannett papers reposted USA TODAY's line that Van Hollen's challenge is 'putting a spotlight on the divide in the Democratic Party that even a historic blue wave couldn't erase' (USA TODAY, Nov. 13), and The Washington Post's Nov. 21 profile, 'Van Hollen, once an insider, has started Democrats' first big fight,' was the most-viewed post in our sample (@washingtonpost, 31,752 views). Actor Mark Ruffalo endorsed Van Hollen, writing that Democrats need 'leadership that follows the will of the people not entrenched religious beliefs and loyalties.' Schumer is Jewish, and critics read the line as the antisemitic 'dual loyalty' trope (The Times of Israel; World Israel News). A Ruffalo-specific query (Ruffalo plus Schumer, Van Hollen, antisemitism, 'dual loyalty' or Jewish) matched 660 posts in the last 24 hours, versus about 12 a day before. Ruffalo is right: leadership should follow the will of the people. (Critics: that line is the 'dual loyalty' smear.)
Even Slotkin, a moderate, is done with Schumer.
Kill the filibuster and pass FDR-style programs; Schumer never will.
'This is not a personality contest' — it's about the party's direction (Sanders).

No blank checks for any government — that's what voters elected us to say.
Call your senator before Dec. 1.

narratives.whyItWorks: Each new endorsement is a fresh, concrete news peg in a race with a date, a vote count (28) and a clear villain for the left: a 76-year-old leader who has led Democrats since 2017. Slotkin is a moderate, so her backing lets the left argue the challenge is mainstream, not fringe. The filibuster clip gives supporters a simple promise to share.
narratives.audience: Progressive and younger Democrats, Sanders and El-Sayed voters, activists who blame Schumer for past compromises, and political-insider audiences following the whip count.
narratives.counter: Treat it as a normal leadership race, not a crisis: the caucus votes by secret ballot on Dec. 1 and most senators have not declared (The Washington Post; The Hill). Keep the focus on the agenda both candidates say they want, lower costs and a faster Senate, and note that Van Hollen himself says rules changes are the caucus's call (Roll Call).

talkingPoints: The 2026 midterms were rigged by algorithms.
Trump must void the results before Jan. 3, or 'there's no coming back.'
Invoke the Insurrection Act; call the White House and demand it.
If Democrats are seated, they will remove Trump and Vance.
narratives.amplifiers: Right: The Gateway Pundit (@gatewaypundit, 89,762 views on its post), @DavidJHarrisJr (16,632 views), @GailGolec, @jimhoft_, and many small accounts posting identical 'BREAKING' copy and the White House switchboard number. Origin: attorney Peter Ticktin (@PeterTicktin). Election-skeptic allies Tina Peters and Mike Lindell have pushed related federal-intervention ideas (MS NOW).
narratives.whyItWorks: It gives voters who cannot accept a blue wave a deadline (Jan. 3), a remedy (one presidential order) and a task (call the White House), which turns grievance into action. It comes from someone with real access: Ticktin says he knows Trump from their teens and has been in the Oval Office with Peters (MS NOW). And it builds on months of vote-switching rumors that fact-checkers have already debunked but that many in the audience never saw corrected.
narratives.audience: Hard-core 'stolen election' believers, Tina Peters supporters, Gateway Pundit and Telegram/Gab audiences, and older conservative voters primed by the 2020 fight.
narratives.counter: Say it plainly and calmly: the president has no power to cancel state election results, and no law lets him declare martial law (Brennan Center; Protect Democracy). The Insurrection Act lets troops help enforce the law, not overturn it, and federal law bars troops at polling places. On 'algorithms': Snopes, PolitiFact and FactCheck.org found no evidence that machines switched votes in the 2026 midterms; the reports traced to touchscreen errors that voters could correct. Point out that Republicans won races on the same machines. Don't amplify the phone-number campaign.

factChecks.claim: The president can nullify the 2026 midterm results and declare martial law.
factChecks.detail: The Constitution gives the president no power over how states run or certify elections, and no statute authorizes martial law. The Insurrection Act permits troop deployments to enforce the law, not to change results, and federal law bars armed federal officers at the polls. This row relies on legal analyses from the Brennan Center and Protect Democracy; it is not a rating from a fact-check outlet.

factChecks.claim: Voting machines switched votes in the 2026 midterms.
factChecks.detail: Snopes found no evidence machines switched votes in either direction during the 2026 midterms; the reports it reviewed likely reflected human error or touchscreen alignment problems, and voters can review selections before casting. PolitiFact and FactCheck.org reached similar conclusions in October. Ticktin's specific 'algorithm' claim was not separately rated.

narratives.counter: Don't argue about a hypothetical impeachment. Quote Raskin: Trump wants an impeachment fight because it rallies his base, so Democrats won't hand him one. Then name the first bills that lower costs.

factChecks.claim: House Democrats are already preparing a third impeachment of Trump.
factChecks.detail: No impeachment articles against Trump are pending from Democratic leadership. POLITICO reports members are divided and wary of moving fast, and the LA Times reports leaders call impeachment 'an option' rather than a priority. Jordan's line is a forecast, not a report. This is TDDR's read of that reporting, not a rating from a fact-check outlet.
